young.html: Suppose you could tell a lie and get something you want, and no one would ever find out. Would it be all right? Immanuel Kant said there is a test you can use.

Ask: What if everybody did this? If everyone told lies whenever it helped them, no one would believe anybody, and lying wouldn't even work anymore. So, Kant said, the rule "lie when it helps me" fails the test.
Kant had a second way to say the same thing: treat people as people, never just as tools for getting what you want. A friend is not a ladder to climb.

young.name: gb-maxim-test
young.cap: Choose a rule for acting and run Kant's test: could everyone follow it?

young.html: The everybody test. Write some rules on cards: "Cut in line when I'm in a hurry," "Say thank you when someone helps me," "Borrow things and never give them back," "Help someone who drops their books." Take turns drawing a card and imagining a world where everyone follows it. Which worlds work? Which ones fall apart?

full.html: Volume 39 gathers Kant's ethics: the Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals (1785; also called the Groundwork), the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), and parts of The Metaphysics of Morals (1797) on law, rights and virtue. Kant wanted to find the supreme principle of morality, one that holds for every rational being, not just for people who happen to want certain things.

full.text: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good without qualification, except a Good Will. Intelligence, wit, judgment, and the other talents of the mind, however they may be named, or courage, resolution, perseverance, as qualities of temperament, are undoubtedly good and desirable in many respects; but these gifts of nature may also become extremely bad and mischievous if the will which is to make use of them… is not good.
full.author: Immanuel Kant
full.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

full.html: A good will is good not because of what it achieves but because of how it wills: it acts from duty, out of respect for the moral law. Kant's example: a shopkeeper who gives children correct change only because it's good for business does the right thing, but his action has no special moral worth. One who would be honest even when it costs him acts from duty.
Many commands are hypothetical: "If you want to be healthy, exercise." They bind only if you want the goal. Morality, Kant says, commands categorically, with no "if":

full.text: There is therefore but one categorical imperative, namely this: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
full.author: Immanuel Kant
full.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

full.html: A maxim is the personal rule behind an action. Kant's test: imagine the maxim as a law everyone follows. Some maxims can't even be thought that way. His example is a lying promise: if everyone made false promises when in need, no one would believe a promise, and the maxim would defeat itself. Others can be thought but not consistently willed, such as never helping anyone, since you yourself will someday need help.

full.name: gb-maxim-test
full.cap: Kant's four examples and more. Run each maxim through the test: can it be a universal law? Could you will it?

full.text: So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only.
full.author: Immanuel Kant
full.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

full.html: Kant thinks this second formula comes to the same thing as the first. A third adds that each rational being is a law-maker in a kingdom of ends: the moral law is not imposed from outside but is reason's own law. That is what Kant calls autonomy, and why he says only beings who give themselves the law have dignity.

The second Critique argues that the moral law shows we are free: "ought" implies "can." Kant also says practical reason must hope that virtue and happiness will finally fit together, which leads him to "postulate" God and the immortality of the soul, not as things proved, but as hopes reason needs for moral life. Its conclusion holds his most famous sentence:

full.text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
full.author: Immanuel Kant
full.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

full.html: Thinking Kant's test asks whether the results would be bad if everyone did something. His first test asks whether the maxim could even work, or be willed without contradiction, as a law for all. It looks at the form of the rule, not at adding up consequences.

deep.html: Kant's strictness drew questions. In a short essay (1797) he said one may not lie even to a murderer asking where a friend is hiding; most readers, including many of his admirers, think this goes too far, and some argue Kant's own principles allow a different answer. Hegel complained that the universal law test is "empty": almost any maxim can be phrased to pass. Utilitarians such as John Stuart Mill, in the next era, judged actions by their consequences for happiness, the main rival to Kant's view ever since.

Defenders reply that Kant captured something many people believe: that persons have a dignity that can't be traded away, that moral rules apply to everyone equally, and that motive matters. The idea of human dignity in many later declarations of rights owes a good deal to him.

items: Is an action good because of its motive, its results, or both?
Can it ever be right to break a promise?
What does it mean to treat someone as an end and not only as a means?

questions: Think of a time you did the right thing even though no one would have known. Why did you?
Is it all right to be nice to someone only because you want something from them?
What if everyone cut in line? What would happen to lines?
Kant said we should treat people as ends, not tools. What's an example of treating someone as a tool?
Kant was amazed by the stars and by the moral law. What fills you with wonder?
